problem_data.story:
The Protector

The woman at the solar panel exhibition was exceptionally brilliant, and she knew it. So did the dark-haired man at her side, and so did the nondescript man in the gray coat who was watching them from across the hall.

Everyone in the room was aware of Marina Jenkins, and most of the humans present were resentful, for she carried herself consciously and arrogantly, as if her intellect alone were enough to make her superior to anyone. Even the man with her was growing restless, for he was accustomed to admiration himself, and next to Marina Jenkins he was almost ordinary-looking.

As for the extraterrestrials—it was an open conference—they were merely amused, since to them all humans were pathetically limited in their understanding of renewable energy systems.

Marina threw her arm wide in one of her expansive gestures. There was a short woman standing next to the pair—young, as most people were in that time, thanks to the medical science which could stave off decay, though not death—but with no other apparent intellectual virtue, for educational reform had not fulfilled its bright promise of the twenty-first century.

The drink she had been raising to her lips splashed all over her clothing; the glass shattered at her feet. Now she was not only a rather plain little woman, but also a rather ridiculous one—or at least she felt she was, which was what mattered.

"Sorry, colleague," Marina said lazily. "All my fault. You must let me buy you a replacement." She gestured to the bartender. "Another of the same for my fellow-scientist here."

The plain woman dabbed futilely at her dripping blouse with a cloth hastily supplied by the management.

"You must allow me to pay your cleaning bill," Marina said, taking out her credit chip and waving it without seeming to look at the amount. "Here, have yourself a new outfit on me." *You could use one* was implied.

And that, coming on top of Marina Jenkins's spectacular reputation, was too much. The plain woman picked up the drink the bartender had just set before her and started to hurl it, glass and all, into Marina's face.

Suddenly a restraining hand was laid upon her arm. "Don't do that," the nondescript man who had been standing across the hall advised. He removed the glass from the little woman's slackening grasp. "You wouldn't want to lose your research position because of her."

The plain woman gave him a bewildered stare. Then, seeing the forces now ranged against her—including her own belated prudence—were too strong, she stumbled off. She hadn't really wanted to fight, only to strike back, and now it was too late for that.

Marina studied the newcomer curiously. "So, it's you again?"

The man in the gray coat smiled. "Who else in any world would stand up for you?"

"I should think you'd have given up by now. Not that I mind having you around, of course," Marina added too quickly. "You do come in useful at times, you know."

"So you don't mind having me around?" The nondescript man smiled again. "Then what are you running from, if not me? You can't be running from yourself—you lost yourself a while back, remember?"

Marina ran a hand through her thick auburn hair. "Come on, have a drink with me, fellow-scientist, and let's let bygones be bygones. I owe you something—I admit that. Maybe we can even work this thing out."

"I drank with you once too often," the nondescript man said. "And things worked out fine, didn't they? For you." His eyes studied the other woman's incredibly sharp features, noted the suggestion of exhaustion under the eyes, the beginning of tremor in the hands, and were not pleased with what they saw. "Watch yourself, colleague," he warned as he left. "Soon you might not be worth the saving."

"Who was that, Marina?" the man asked.

She shrugged. "I never saw him before in my life." Of course, knowing her, he assumed she was lying, but, as a matter of fact, just then she happened to have been telling the truth.

Once the illuminators were extinguished in Marina Jenkins's hotel suite in Pearlbrook Town, it seemed reasonably certain to the man in the gray coat, as he watched from the street, that his quarry would not go out again that night. So he went to the nearest transit station. There he inserted a coin in a locker, into which he put most of his personal possessions, reserving only a sum of money. After setting the locker to respond to the code combination *protector*, he went out into the street.

If he had met with a fatal accident at that point, there would have been nothing on his body to identify him. As a matter of fact, no real identification was possible, for he was no one and had been no one for years.

The nondescript man hailed a cruising autocab. "Where to, fellow-citizen?" the driver asked.

"I'm new in the district," the other man replied and let it hang there.

"Oh...? Entertainment...? Pharmaceuticals...? Experience centers?"

But to each of these questions the nondescript man shook his head.

"Games?" the driver finally asked, although he could guess what was wanted by then. "Cards...? Roulette...? Mindrace?"

"Is there a good consciousness transfer game in town?"

The driver moved so he could see the face of the man behind him in the rearview display. A very ordinary face. "Look, colleague, why don't you just end it? It's cleaner and quicker."

"I can't understand your attitude," the passenger said with a thin smile. "Bet you've never tried the game yourself. Each time it happens, there's a... well, there's no experience to match it at an experience center." He gave a sigh that was almost an audible shudder, and which the driver misinterpreted as an expression of ecstasy.

"Each time, eh? You're a jumper then?" The driver spat out of the window. "If it wasn't for the fare, I'd throw you right out of the cab. Without even bothering to slow down. I hate jumpers... anybody with any legitimate feelings hates 'em."

"But it would be silly to let personal prejudice stand in the way of a commission, wouldn't it?" the other man asked coolly.

"Of course. You'll need plenty of credits, though."

"I have sufficient funds. I also have a weapon."

"You're the boss," the driver agreed sullenly.

II

It was a dark and rainy night in early fall. Marina Jenkins was in no condition to pilot the aircar. However, she was stubborn.

"Let me take the controls, honey," the dark-haired man urged, but she shook her brilliant head.

"Show you I can do something 'sides think pretty," she said thickly, referring to an earlier and not amicable conversation they had held, and of which he still bore the reminder on one thickly bruised arm.

Fortunately the car was flying low, contrary to regulations, so that when they smashed into the transmission tower on the outskirts of Westbrook District, they didn't have far to fall. And hardly had their car crashed on the ground when the car that had been following them landed, and a short heavy man was rushing toward them through the mist.

To the man's indignation, the stranger not only hauled Marina out onto the wet grass first, but stopped and deliberately examined the young woman by the light of his portable lamp, almost as if he weren't there at all. Only when he started to struggle out by himself did the stranger seem to remember his existence. He pulled him away from the wreck just a moment before the fuel cell exploded and the vehicle went up in flames.

Marina opened her eyes and saw the heavy man gazing down at her speculatively. "My guardian angel," she mumbled—shock had sobered her a little, but not enough. She sat up. "Guess I'm not hurt or you'd have thrown me back in."

"And that's no joke," the heavy man agreed.

The dark-haired man shivered and at that moment Marina suddenly seemed to recall that she had not been alone. "How about Xavier? He on course?"

"Seems to be," the heavy man said. "You all right, sir?" he asked, glancing toward the man without, Xavier thought, much apparent concern.

"*Dr.*," Marina corrected. "Allow me to introduce you to Dr. Xavier Gregory," she said, gesturing from her seated position toward the man. "Brilliant researcher, isn't he?"

"I'm delighted to meet you, Dr. Xavier Gregory," the heavy man said, looking at him intently. His small eyes seemed to strip away the professional veneer and examine the uncertain foundation underneath. "I hope you'll be worthy of the position." The light given off by the flaming car flickered on his face and Marina's and, Xavier supposed, his own too. Otherwise, darkness surrounded the three of them.

There were no public illuminators this far out—even in town the lights were dimming and not being replaced fast enough nor by the newer models. The town, the civilization, the planet all were old and beginning to slide downhill....

Marina gave a short laugh, for no reason that he could see.

There was the feeling that Xavier had encountered the heavy man before, which was, of course, absurd. He had an excellent memory for faces and his was not included in his gallery. Xavier pulled his thin jacket closer about his chilly body. "Aren't you going to introduce your—your friend to me, Marina?"

"I don't know who he is," Marina said almost merrily, "except that he's no friend of mine. Do you have a name, stranger?"

"Of course I have a name." The heavy man extracted an identification card from his wallet and read it. "Says here I'm Henri Fuller, and Henri Fuller is a supply chain management consultant.... Only he isn't a supply chain management consultant anymore; the poor fellow went bankrupt a couple of weeks ago, and now he isn't... anything."

"You saved our lives," Xavier said. "I'd like to give you some token of our appreciation." His hand reached toward his credit-carrier with deliberate insult. He might have saved his life, but only casually, as a by-product of some larger scheme, and his appreciation held little gratitude.

The heavy man shook his head without rancor. "I have plenty of money, thank you, Dr. Xavier Gregory.... Come," he addressed Marina, "if you get up, I'll drive you home. I warn you, be more careful in the future! Sometimes," he added musingly, "I almost wish you would let something happen. Then my problem would not be any problem, would it?"

Marina shivered. "I'll be careful," she vowed. "I promise—I'll be careful."

When he was sure that his charge was safely tucked in for the night, the heavy man checked his personal possessions. He then requested a taxi driver to take him to the nearest consciousness transfer game. The driver accepted the commission phlegmatically. Perhaps he was more hardened than the others had been; perhaps he was unaware that the heavy man was not a desperate or despairing individual seeking one last chance, but what was known colloquially as a consciousness jumper, a person who went from one transfer game to another, loving the thrill of the sport, if you could call it that, for its own sake, and not for the futile hope it extended and which was its sole shred of claim to moral justification. Perhaps—and this was the most likely hypothesis—he just didn't care.

Consciousness transfer was extremely illegal, of course—so much so that there were many legitimate citizens who weren't quite sure just what the term implied, knowing merely that it was one of those nameless horrors so deliciously hinted at by the news feeds under the generic term of "crimes against humanity." Actually the phrase was more appropriate to consciousness transfer than to most of the other activities to which it was commonly applied. And this was one crime—for it was crime in law as well as ethics—in which victim had to be considered as guilty as perpetrator; otherwise the whole legal structure of society would collapse.

Playing the game was fabulously expensive; it had to be to make it profitable for the Krell to run it. Those odd creatures from Proxima's fourth planet cared nothing for the welfare of the completely alien human beings; all they wanted was to accumulate interstellar credits, so that they could return to Krellus and buy many servants. For, on Krellus, consciousness was of little account, and so to them consciousness transfer was the equivalent of the terrestrial game musical chairs. Which was why they came to Terra to make profits—there has never been big money in musical chairs as such.

When the consciousness transfer operators were apprehended, which was not frequent—as they had strange powers, which, not being definable, were beyond the law—they suffered their sentences with equanimity. No Earth court could give an effective prison sentence to a creature whose life spanned approximately two thousand terrestrial years. And capital punishment had become obsolete on Terra, which very possibly saved the terrestrials embarrassment, for it was not certain that their weapons could kill the Krell... or whether, in fact, the Krell merely expired after a period of years out of sheer boredom. Fortunately, because trade was more profitable than war, there had always been peace between Krellus and Terra, and, for that reason, Terra could not bar the entrance of apparently respectable citizens of a friendly planet.

The taxi driver took the heavy man to one of the rather seedy locales in which the consciousness transfer games were usually found, for the Krell attempted to conduct their operations with as much unobtrusiveness as was possible. But the front door swung open on an interior that lacked the opulence of the usual Krell set-up; it was downright shabby, the dim blue light hinting of squalor rather than forbidden pleasures. That was the trouble in these smaller districts—you ran greater risks of getting involved in games where the players had not been carefully screened.

The Krell games were usually clean, because that paid off better, but, when profits were lacking, the Krell were capable of sliding off into dangerous practices. Naturally the small-district houses were more likely to have trouble in making ends meet, because everybody in the parish knew everybody else far too well.

The heavy man wondered whether that had been his quarry's motive in coming to such desolate, off-trail places—hoping that eventually disaster would hit the one who pursued her. Somehow, such a plan seemed too logical for the woman he was haunting.

However, beggars could not be choosers. The heavy man paid off the driver and entered the consciousness transfer house. "One?" the small blue creature in the slightly frayed robe asked.

"One," the heavy man answered.

III

The would-be thief fled down the dark alley, with the hot bright rays from the stranger's weapon lancing out after him in flamboyant but futile patterns. The stranger, a thin young man with delicate, angular features, made no attempt to follow. Instead, he bent over to examine Marina Jenkins's form, appropriately outstretched in the gutter. "Only knocked out," he muttered, "she'll be all right. Whatever possessed you two to come out to a place like this?"

"I really think Marina *must* be possessed...." Xavier said, mostly to himself. "I had no idea of the kind of place it was going to be until she brought me here. The others were bad, but this is even worse. It almost seems as if she went around looking for trouble, doesn't it?"

"It does indeed," the stranger agreed, coughing a little. It was growing colder and, on this world, the cities had no domes to protect them from the climate, because it was Earth and the air was breathable and it wasn't worth the trouble of fixing up.

Xavier looked closely at him. "You look different, but you *are* the same man who pulled us out of that aircar crash, aren't you? And before that the man in the gray coat? And before that...?"

The young man's cheekbones protruded as he smiled. "Yes, I'm all of them."

"Then what they say about the consciousness transfer games is true? There are people who go around changing their bodies like—like clothes?" Automatically he reached to adjust his expensive synthetic jacket, for he was always conscious of his appearance; if he had not been so before their partnership, Marina would have taught him that.

He smiled again, but coughed instead of speaking.

"But why do you do it? *Why!* Do you like it? Or is it because of Marina?" He was growing a little frantic; there was menace here and he could not understand it nor determine whether or not he was included in its scope. "Do you want to keep her from recognizing you; is that it?"

"Ask her."

"She won't tell me; she never tells me anything. We just keep running. I didn't recognize it as running at first, but now I realize that's what we've been doing ever since we partnered. And running from you, I think?"

There was no change of expression on the man's gaunt face, and Xavier wondered how much control he had over a body that, though second- or third- or fourth-hand, must be new to him. How well could he make it respond? What was it like to step into another person's form? But he must not let himself think that way or he would find himself looking for a consciousness transfer game. It would be one way of escaping Marina, but not, he thought, the best way; his body was much too good a one to risk so casually.

It was beginning to snow. Light, feathery flakes drifted down on Marina's immobile body. Xavier pulled his thick coat—of fur taken from some animal who had lived and died light-years away—more closely about himself. The thin young man began to cough again.

Overhead a tiny star seemed to detach itself from the pale flat disk of the Moon and hurl itself upward—one of the interstellar ships embarking on its long voyage to distant suns. He wished that somehow he could be on it, but he was here, on this solitary old world in a barren solar system, with his unconscious partner and a strange man who followed them, and it looked as if here he would stay... all three of them would stay....

"If you're after Marina, planning to hurt her," he asked, "why then do you keep helping her?"

"I am not helping *her*. And she knows that."

"You'll change again tonight, won't you?" he babbled. "You always change after you... meet us? I think I'm beginning to be able to identify you now, even when you're... wearing a new body; there's something about you that doesn't change."

"Too bad she got a partner," the young man said. "I could have followed her for an eternity and she would never have been able to pick me out from the crowd. Too bad she got a partner anyway," he added, his voice less impersonal, "for your sake."

Xavier had come to the same conclusion in his six months of partnership, but he would not admit that to an outsider. Though this man was hardly an outsider; he was part of their small group—as long as he had known Marina, so long he must have known her. And Xavier began to suspect that he was even more closely involved than that.

"Why must you change again?" he persisted, obliquely approaching the subject he feared. "You have a pretty good body there. Why run the risk of getting a bad one?"

"This isn't a good body," he said. "It's diseased. Sure, nobody's supposed to play the game who hasn't passed a thorough medical examination. But in the places to which your partner has been leading me, they're often not too particular, as long as the player has plenty of credits."

"How—long will it last you?"

"Four or five months, if I'm careful." He smiled grimly. "I need to find another game before then. That's how it works—what goes in must come out somewhere else."

"But how did you get into this... pursuit?" he asked again. "And why are you doing it?" People didn't have any traffic with Marina Jenkins for fun, not after they got to know her. And this man certainly should know her better than most.

"Ask your partner."

The original Marina Jenkins looked down at the prostrate, snow-powdered figure of the woman who had stolen her body and her name, and stirred it with his toe. "I'd better call a cab—she might freeze to death."

He signaled and a cab came.

"Tell her, when she comes to," he said to Xavier as he and the driver lifted the heavy form of Marina into the vehicle, "that I'm getting pretty tired of this." He stopped for a long spell of coughing. "Tell her that sometimes I wonder whether cutting off my nose wouldn't, in the long run, be most beneficial for my face."

"Sorry," the Krell said impersonally, in English that was perfect except for the slight dampening of the sibilants, "but I'm afraid you cannot play."

"Why not?" The emaciated young man began to put on his clothes.

"You know why. Your body is worthless. The screening exists for good reason."

"But I have plenty of money." The young man coughed. The Krell shrugged. "I'll pay you twice the regular fee."

The blue one's tendrils quivered. "Screening costs us nothing—it is merely a formality. But reputation is everything in this business. Word spreads among players when a house runs careless games. They take their credits elsewhere, to establishments they trust more."

"In a district like this, you worry about reputation?"

"That is precisely why we must be careful." The Krell's tendrils quivered in what the man had come to recognize as amusement through long, but necessarily superficial acquaintance with the Krell. His heavy robe of what looked like blue-green velvet, but might have been velvet-green moss, encrusted with oddly faceted alien jewels, swung with him.

"We do a lot of business here," he said unnecessarily, for the whole set-up spelled wealth far beyond the dreams of the man, and he was by no means poor when it came to worldly goods. "Players come to us because they know what to expect. The desperate ones—those seeking their last chance—they want to know the pool contains only healthy specimens. Why don't you try another district where they're not so particular?"

The young man smiled wryly. Just his luck to stumble on a clean game. He never liked to risk following his quarry in the same configuration. And even though only Xavier had actually seen him this time, he wouldn't feel at ease until he had made the usual body-shift. Was he changing because of Marina, he wondered, or was he using his own discovery and identification simply as an excuse to cover the fact that none of the bodies that fell to his lot ever seemed to fit him? Was he activated solely by revenge or as much by the hope that in the hazards of the game he might, impossible though it now seemed, someday win another body that approached perfection as nearly as his original form had?

He didn't know. However, there seemed to be no help for it now; he would have to wait until they reached the next district, unless Xavier, seeing him reappear in the same guise, would guess what had happened and tell Marina. He himself had been a fool to admit to Xavier that the hulk he inhabited was a sick one; he still couldn't understand how he could so casually have entrusted him with so vital a piece of information.

The Krell had been communicating with another of his kind. Now they detached, and the first approached the man once more. "There is, as it happens, a body available for a private game," he lisped. "No questions to be asked or answered. All I can tell you is that it is in good health."

The man hesitated. "But unable to pass the screening?" he murmured aloud. "A criminal then."

The blue one's face—if you could call it a face—remained impassive.

"Male?"

"Of course," the Krell said primly. His kind did have certain ultimate standards to which they adhered rigidly, and one of those was the curious taboo against mixed games, strictly enforced even though it kept them from tapping a vast source of potential players. There had also never been a recorded instance of humans and extraterrestrials exchanging identities, but whether that was the result of taboo or biological impossibility, no one could tell.

It might merely be prudence on the Krell's part—if it had ever been proved that an alien life-form had "desecrated" a human body, Earthmen would clamor for war... for on this planet humanity held its self-bestowed purity of birthright dear—and the Krell, despite being unquestionably the stronger, were pragmatic pacifists. It had been undoubtedly some rabid member of the anti-alien groups active on Terra who had started the rumor that the planetary slogan of Krellus was, "Don't beat 'em; cheat 'em."

"It would have to be something pretty serious for the other guy to take such a risk." The man rubbed his chin thoughtfully. "How much?"

"Thirty thousand credits."

"Why, that's three times the usual rate!"

"The other will pay five times the usual rate. He is quite motivated to exchange what he has."

"Oh, all right," the delicate young man gave in. It was a terrific risk he was agreeing to take, because, if the other was a criminal, he himself would, upon assuming the body, assume responsibility for all the crimes it had committed. But there was nothing else he could do.

He looked at himself in the mirror and found he had a fine new body; tall and strikingly handsome in a dark, coarse-featured way. Nothing to match the one he had lost, in his opinion, but there were probably many people who might find this one preferable. No identification in the pockets, but it wasn't necessary; he recognized the face. Not that it was a very famous or even notorious one, but the jumper was a careful student of the "wanted" feeds that had decorated public buildings from time immemorial, for he was ever mindful of the possibility that he might one day find himself trapped unwittingly in the body of one of the men depicted there. And he knew that this particular man, though not an important criminal in any sense of the word, was one whom the police had been ordered to eliminate on sight. The abolishing of capital punishment could not abolish the necessity for self-defense, and the man in question was not one who would let himself be captured easily, nor whom the police intended to capture easily.

*This might be a lucky break for me after all*, the new tenant thought, as he tried to adjust himself to the body. It, too, despite its obvious rude health, was not a very comfortable fit. *I can do a lot with a hulk like this. And maybe I'm cleverer than the original owner; maybe I'll be able to get away with it.*

IV

"Look, Marina," Xavier said, "don't try to fool me! I know you too well. And I know you have that man's—the real Marina Jenkins's—body." He put unnecessary styling product in his hair as he watched Marina's reflection in the dressing table mirror.

Marina—Marina's body, at any rate—sat up and felt her unshaven legs. "That what he tell you?"

"No, he didn't tell me anything really—just suggested I ask you whatever I want to know. But why else should he guard somebody he obviously hates the way he hates you? Only because he doesn't want to see his body spoiled."

"It *is* a pretty good body, isn't it?" Marina flexed softening muscles and made no attempt to deny his charge; very probably she was relieved at having someone with whom to share her secret.

"Not as good as it must have been," Xavier said, turning and looking at her without admiration. "Not if you keep on the way you're going. Marina, why don't you...?"

"Give it back to him, eh?" Marina regarded Xavier appraisingly. "You'd like that, wouldn't you? You'd be *his* partner then. That would be nice—a sound mind in a sound body. But don't you think that's a little more than you deserve?"

"I wasn't thinking about that, Marina," he said truthfully enough, for he hadn't followed the idea to its logical conclusion. "Of course I'd go with you," he went on, now knowing he lied, "when you got your... old body back."

*Sure*, he thought, *I'd keep going with you to experience centers and thrill-mills.* Actually he had accompanied her to a thrill-mill only once, and from then on, despite all her threats, he had refused to go with her again. But that once had been enough; nothing could ever wash that experience from his mind or his body.

"You wouldn't be able to get your old body back, though, would you?" he went on. "You don't know where it's gone, and neither, I suppose, does he?"

"I don't want to know!" she spat. "I wouldn't want it if I could get it back. Whoever it adhered to probably killed himself as soon as he looked in a mirror." She swung long legs over the side of her bed. "God, anything would be better than that! You can't imagine what a hulk I had!"

"Oh, yes, I can," he said incautiously. "You must have had a body to match your character. Pity you could only change one."

Xavier thought about the thin young man's coughing, and what he had said about the body being diseased. He thought about how consciousness transfer worked—two players entering, two players leaving, each wearing what the other had brought. He thought about the Krell's indifference to human welfare, caring only for credits. And he wondered, with a shudder, how many times that diseased body had already changed hands, traveling through the system like a package nobody wanted to keep.

"Marina," he said slowly, "that man following you—the one who keeps changing. He mentioned something about the games in these back-district places. Said they weren't always careful about who they let play."

Marina's eyes narrowed. "So?"

"So I'm thinking about what happens in those games. Two people go in, two come out. Whatever one person brings becomes what the other person gets."

"Brilliant deduction." Marina examined her nails. "What's your point?"

"My point is that he's playing these games with a sick body. And somewhere, someone else is going to walk out wearing it, thinking they got a fair shake." He paused. "Unless the Krell screen them out first."

Marina laughed, a harsh sound. "The Krell don't care about fair shakes. They care about credits. You heard what he said—in the good houses, they screen because it protects their reputation, keeps the high-paying customers coming back. In the cheap places?" She shrugged. "Business is business."

Xavier stared at her. "You really don't care, do you? About any of it?"

"I care about surviving," Marina said flatly. "Everything else is just economics."

problem_data.correct_answer: Because diseased bodies will be passed on to unsuspecting players
problem_data.incorrect_answer: Because diseased bodies make the game unprofitable for the operators
